presenceNote: The Potawatomi homeland is the Great Lakes (Michigan, Wisconsin, northern Indiana and Illinois), outside Kentucky and mostly outside this map, so it is described in text and not drawn. The story itself has no dates; the page spans c.1640 (Beaver Wars refuge) to 1809 (Fort Wayne cession). The Kentucky link is the 1791 Scott and Wilkinson expeditions against Wea and Miami neighbours, and Potawatomi warriors in the Confederacy; the story names no Potawatomi raid on a Kentucky station.
overlapNote: Miami, Wea, Kickapoo, Ojibwe and Odawa (Three Fires), Illinois (their country was taken from the Illinois), Menominee and Ho-Chunk in Wisconsin. In the 1805 Grouseland treaty they acknowledged the Delaware right to sell; in 1809 they ceded with the Delaware, Miami and Eel River.
basis: Illinois State Museum (Midewin exhibit), NHBP timeline, Indiana DNR, Forest County Potawatomi (Wisconsin DPI), Greenville and Fort Wayne treaty references.

eras.label: c.1640–1670 · Beaver Wars refuge
eras.text: By the 1640s the Potawatomi were under Iroquois attack and fled north to the Straits of Mackinac and to Green Bay and Door County, Wisconsin, where they built French trade alliances and, by 1670, began to expand (Illinois State Museum). Wisconsin is outside this map, so this period is text only.

eras.label: c.1763–1795 · Southern Michigan, northern Indiana and Illinois
eras.text: The Detroit Potawatomi left their river villages in 1763 and set up villages on the Huron River and the Raisin; Indiana DNR has Potawatomi moving as far south as the Wabash in the 1770s. By the 1800s there were over 100 villages, 14 of them in northern and central Illinois (Illinois State Museum). Only two points (Detroit and Chicago) are drawn; the homeland extent is text only. Potawatomi warriors stood in the Northwest Indian Confederacy; Kentucky’s 1791 columns under Scott and Wilkinson struck their Wea and Miami neighbours, not Potawatomi towns.

eras.label: 1795–1809 · Greenville and the Chicago cession
eras.text: At Greenville (3 Aug 1795) the Potawatomi signed, took $1,000 a year and ceded six miles square at Chicago among the posts. On 30 Sept 1809 at Fort Wayne the Delaware, Potawatomi, Miami and Eel River ceded about 2.5 million acres along the Wabash (EBSCO; acreage varies by source, 2.5 to 3 million).
